The U.S. doesn’t actually have a “healthcare system.”
We have a billing system with healthcare attached to it.

Fix the root causes…

1. Prices Are Completely Unregulated and Opaque

The U.S. is the only high-income country where hospitals, insurers, and drug companies can charge whatever they want with no standardized price list.
Two people can get the same procedure and one gets billed $1,200 while the other gets hit with $14,000. No other major industry could get away with this.

Core issue: no transparency, no caps, and no competitive pressure.

2. Administrative Bloat – Too Many Middlemen

About 25–30% of U.S. healthcare spending goes to admin costs: billing departments, coding teams, claim reviewers, prior authorization layers, endless insurance paperwork.

Other countries run their systems with half or even one-third of that overhead.

Core issue: the system is designed for billing complexity, not patient care.

3. Employer-Based Insurance Locks Everyone Into a Bad Model

Tying insurance to your job made sense in the 1940s. Today it traps people:
•Lose your job → lose your healthcare
•Small businesses get crushed by premiums
•No incentive for insurers to keep long-term patient costs down, because people switch jobs every few years

Core issue: the financing structure is outdated and creates churn instead of stability.

4. No Real Competition in Many Markets

In half the country, one or two hospital systems control everything. Same with insurers. When markets consolidate, prices go up and quality doesn’t improve.

Core issue: healthcare acts like a monopoly, not a marketplace.

5. Fee-for-Service Incentives Reward Quantity, Not Outcomes

Doctors and hospitals get paid for doing more tests, more scans, more procedures — even if they aren’t necessary.
There’s no bonus for keeping someone healthy.
There is a bonus for doing an MRI, even when a cheaper test would do.

Core issue: misaligned incentives drive overbilling and overtreatment.

6. Drug Prices Are Sky-High Because There’s No Negotiation

The U.S. lets pharma companies set whatever prices they want and bars Medicare from negotiating on most drugs (though this is finally starting to change).

Same medications cost 50–80% less in Europe, Canada, and Asia.

Core issue: government barred itself from using buying power.

7. Chronic Disease Drives the Majority of Costs

Diabetes, heart disease, obesity, smoking-related illness — these account for over 80% of total healthcare spending.

We treat sickness aggressively but invest almost nothing in prevention or early intervention.

Core issue: no incentive to keep people healthy until they’re already sick.

8. Insurance Networks Create Artificial Barriers to Care

In-network, out-of-network, surprise billing, narrow networks — it’s a system designed to save insurers money, not patients.

Core issue: even people with insurance can’t access half the care they need.

9. Rural Access Is Collapsing

Hospitals are closing across rural America. Provider shortages mean many counties have:
•No OB-GYN
•No psychiatrist
•No primary care physician

When people delay care, costs skyrocket later.

Core issue: care deserts create downstream costs and worse outcomes.

10. Political Paralysis & Lobbying Power

Healthcare lobbying spends more money than oil, defense, and tech combined.
Reform dies in Congress every time because:
•Insurers fight price regulation
•Pharma fights negotiation
•Hospitals fight competition
•Politicians avoid big changes

Core issue: everyone profits from the system staying broken — except patients.
